# Psalm 74: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I couldn't find:** My searches turned up nothing from Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox (oca.org), Pentecostal denominational (ag.org) or Anglican sources. I also found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers on this psalm, so those views are left out. I read two pages in full: Enduring Word (David Guzik) and the Pulpit Commentary on StudyLight. Points taken from those two pages have a URL but no quotation tag.

---

**Background: date and author**
- Guzik says most commentators date the psalm after Babylon destroyed the temple, and some date it later, to Antiochus Epiphanes. A third option is that David's Asaph wrote it about the fall of Shiloh (1 Samuel 4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- The Pulpit Commentary rules out both the Shishak and Maccabean dates and settles on the time just after Nebuchadnezzar took the city. It explains the title by saying "Asaph" became a family or guild name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Coffman lists three proposed dates: 587 BC, Artaxerxes Ochus in 351 BC, and Antiochus in 167 BC. Despite the skillful arguments of Delitzsch who favored the Maccabean date, he concludes for 587 BC. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-74.html
- Constable says the writer was an Asaph who lived much later than David's day, or perhaps Asaph stands for the order of musicians he headed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-74.html
- Utley (bible.org) gives two possible settings: Babylon in 586 BC, or the invasion of Edom in 485 b.c., where the temple was defiled and damaged. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-74

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary says only extreme distress could make a devout Israelite think Israel was cast off forever. God's anger "smokes" when it burns hot, and the "sheep of your pasture" are his own flock. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik, quoting Morgan, Kidner and VanGemeren, reads the cry as faith rather than unbelief: a lament that appeals to God's fatherly heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- **Catholic (Augustine, who uses the Latin numbering, Ps 73):** Augustine reads "Asaph" as meaning "congregation" or "synagogue." He says the speaker censures not, but inquires wherefore. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes "purchased of old" as the redemption from Egypt (Exodus 15:16). It says "this Mount Zion" suggests the writer was still in the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik lists the grounds the psalmist pleads: congregation, purchase, inheritance and God's dwelling. He quotes Spurgeon's view of redemption as a mighty plea. He also notes Poole's view that "tribe of your inheritance" means Judah in particular. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- Augustine says the congregation God possessed "from the beginning" is Israel according to the flesh. Christians become its children not by coming out of their flesh, but by imitating their faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary: God is asked to come and inspect the ruins. It argues that neither Shishak nor Antiochus caused damage on this scale. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik reads "lift up your feet" as a plea for God to hurry to help. He also lists ways to explain the "perpetual desolations" under different authorship theories. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/

**v. 4**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the roaring as battle-cries and shouts of victory in the temple. It takes the banners as signs of victory and rule, probably not objects of worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik cites Kidner: the "signs" are military standards. He also cites Spurgeon, who applies the verse to false teaching heard from once-faithful pulpits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- Augustine applies the verse to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem: their standards, their eagles, their own dragons, the Roman signs. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm

**vv. 5–6**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the enemy swung hatchets as carelessly as men cutting a thicket. The carvings were the cherubim, palms and flowers of 1 Kings 6:29, perhaps hacked off for their gold. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Coffman: the soldiers attacked the sanctuary just like a company of woodsmen chopping down a grove of trees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-74.html
- **Modern scholarship:** Utley cites Dahood (Anchor Bible), who calls these verses among the most obscure and difficult of the entire Psalter. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-74

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Nebuchadnezzar burned Solomon's temple (2 Kings 25:9). Zerubbabel's temple was never burned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Ellicott notes that 1 Maccabees and Josephus say Judas Maccabeus found that the gates had been burnt. That detail is relevant to the Maccabean-date argument. https://biblehub.com/psalms/74-7.htm
- **Dispensational (McGee):** the verse looks forward also to another day that's coming when the temple will be rebuilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-8.html

**v. 8**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Nebuchadnezzar meant to destroy Israel as a nation. On "meeting places" (KJV "synagogues"), it argues that places of worship outside the temple existed before the Exile, so the word does not prove a Maccabean date. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik, citing Clarke and Boice, says there were probably local places for prayer and Scripture before formal synagogues existed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin accepts the word in the sense of synagogues, because he says ALL the sanctuaries. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-8.html
- The Restoration Commentary calls "synagogues" a mistranslation, since synagogues are usually tied to the Maccabean era. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-74.html

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes "signs" as God's ordinances: tabernacle, sacrifices, sabbaths. "No prophet" means none in Palestine, even though Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel were alive elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- **Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke says there were prophets in the captivity, but none who travelled the land preaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-9.html
- Barnes: the phrase means no messenger of comfort had come, not that no prophet existed at all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-9.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill extends the silence to after Malachi and the time of Antiochus, until John the Baptist. He also applies it to the two witnesses of Revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-9.html
- Augustine applies the verse to Jews who still wait for the Messiah. Christ came once to call and will come as Judge. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm

**vv. 10–11**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the two questions are "will this last forever?" and "if not, how long?" On v. 11 it says the psalmist [no direct support]… (correction: no citation available) — in its own words, the psalmist does not grasp how great Israel's sin was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik: the psalmist never doubted God's power, only why God held it back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- Utley: If the invader is Babylon then YHWH is fighting on their side. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-74

**v. 12**
- The Pulpit Commentary: as King, God can deliver. "In the midst of the earth" means in many places, not some imagined centre of the earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik, quoting Morgan, calls this the turn from what the eye sees to what faith sees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/

**vv. 13–14 (dragons and Leviathan): the most debated verses**
- **Traditional reading (Egypt):** The Pulpit Commentary says the dragon is frequently used as a symbol of Egyptian power and points to Pharaoh's army drowning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/74-13.htm. Matthew Henry agrees: Pharaoh was the leviathan; the Egyptians were the dragons. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_074.cfm. Wesley's Notes take the same line. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-13.html
- **Who were "the creatures of the desert"?** The commentators disagree:
  - Constable: The creatures of the wilderness are the Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-14.html
  - Barnes denies this. He says the image is entirely poetic. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/74-14.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the "meat" is the Egyptian dead washed ashore. https://biblehub.com/psalms/74-14.htm
  - Henry calls it part of Israel's "spiritual meat." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_074.cfm
- **Spiritual reading:** One commentary quoted on StudyLight adds that Satan is the dragon whose head Christ bruised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-13.html. Augustine says the dragons are demons and their chief is the devil himself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801074.htm
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - NET Bible notes say the imagery originates in West Semitic mythology and cite Ugaritic texts about a seven-headed serpent. They suggest the plural "dragons" may come from a misread enclitic *mem* (a Hebrew suffix), so the original may have meant one monster. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+74:12-15
  - Bible Odyssey: in Ugaritic myth Leviathan (Lothan) is one of the primeval sea monsters who battles against Baal. https://blog.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/leviathan/
  - Guzik, an evangelical, accepts this background. He says the biblical writers reworked the myths to show that Yahweh alone defeats these forces. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- **Catholic text:** The Douay-Rheims (translated from the Latin Vulgate) reads meat for the people of the Ethiopians. https://biblehub.com/psalms/74-14.htm

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary: water from the rock (Exodus 17; Numbers 20) and the drying of the Jordan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Constable says the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-14.html

**vv. 16–17**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the psalm moves from God's acts in history to his rule over nature, echoing Genesis 1. The "borders" are the limits between land and sea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- Guzik notes that the day/night and sun language points to creation more than to Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/

**v. 18**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew word for "foolish" is *nabal*, a folly close to wickedness. Every idol-worshipping nation is "foolish" whatever its intelligence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html

**v. 19**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Israel is God's pet dove, and Babylon is the greedy crowd ready to devour it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
- **Catholic text:** The Douay-Rheims reads Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee. https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/74-20.htm

**v. 20 (the clearest split between traditions)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** the only firm ground for prayer is that God has adopted us to be his people by his free choice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-20.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** the covenant is the covenant of grace made with Christ. The "dark places" are lands of Pagans, Mahometans, and Papists, and the verse is a prayer for the gospel to spread. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/74-20.htm
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik):** plead the covenant "of which Jesus is the Mediator." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-74/
- **Methodist:**
  - Wesley: the covenant with Abraham that gave him Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-20.html
  - Clarke: the covenant sacrifice of Genesis 15, An indisputable type of Jesus Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-20.html
- **Others:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary: the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The dark places are pagan lands where captives are treated cruelly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/74-20.htm
  - Clarke and Coffman take the dark places as caves where the persecuted hid. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/74-20.html
- **Modern scholarship:** Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible suggest small changes to the Hebrew text. Delitzsch links the hiding-places to the Maccabean persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/74-20.htm

**v. 21**
- The Pulpit Commentary: let the oppressed not turn away ashamed that God has forsaken them, but receive mercy that turns shame into praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html

**v. 22**
- The Pulpit Commentary: in the ancient world, conquering a people counted as a victory over its gods. So the insult is aimed at God himself. Its sermon notes add that the cause of God's church is God's own cause. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html

**v. 23**
- The Pulpit Commentary: God does not forget such insults (2 Kings 19:28) and later punished Babylon. Their uproar "ascends" to God's throne, crying for justice, like Abel's blood (Genesis 4:10). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-74.html
